description: We are a small team of college students interested in space science, technology, data analysis, and problem-solving. We aim to collaborate, explore innovative ideas, and develop a meaningful solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We value teamwork, creativity, curiosity, and a willingness to learn while working together on this challenge.
summary:
**SpaceVerse: Beyond the Final Signal**

SpaceVerse is an interactive digital archive developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge *Abandoned but Not Forgotten*. It explores the stories and scientific legacy of spacecraft, rovers and scientific equipment left behind after space missions.

The platform organizes 17 curated mission and artifact records across three categories: Moon, Mars and Deep Space. Visitors can explore mission histories, objectives, operational status, resting places and scientific contributions through an interactive mission archive. It also features a NASA-powered image gallery, an educational quiz and dedicated sections explaining the project's purpose and research.

SpaceVerse addresses the challenge by bringing scattered information about historic space missions into one accessible platform, helping people discover what remains after humanity's journeys into space. It is important because the end of a mission does not mean the end of its story. Preserving these records helps us appreciate past scientific achievements, understand the legacy of space exploration and recognize the importance of responsible future missions.
details:
SpaceVerse: Beyond the Final Signal

What does the project do and how does it work?

SpaceVerse is an interactive digital archive that explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific instruments that remain after space missions end. It organizes selected mission records into three collections: Moon, Mars and Deep Space.

Visitors can explore the destination-based Explorer, browse the Mission and Artifact Archive, search records by mission name, target, status or resting place, and expand individual entries to learn about their objectives, histories, scientific contributions and known final locations. Each record includes links to its research sources. The platform also features a NASA image gallery that retrieves images and metadata from NASA's public Image and Video Library API, along with an interactive educational quiz.

What benefits does it provide?

SpaceVerse makes information about historic space missions easier to discover and understand by bringing selected records together in one accessible platform. It connects mission history with scientific achievements, the long-term presence of human-made objects in space, orbital debris concerns and planetary protection.

What is its intended impact?

The project's intended impact is to encourage people to look beyond the launch and operational life of a spacecraft and appreciate what remains afterward. It aims to preserve the scientific and historical legacy of space exploration, increase public awareness and encourage more responsible thinking about future space missions.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5: Structure of the website and its individual pages.
  • CSS3: Responsive layouts, visual styling, animations and the dark space-inspired interface.
  • JavaScript: Interactive navigation, mission searching, category filtering, expandable mission details and quiz functionality.
  • Three.js: Animated starfield background to create an immersive space environment.
  • NASA Image and Video Library API: Retrieval of public NASA mission photographs and associated metadata.
  • JSON and CSV: Storage and organization of the curated Moon, Mars and Deep Space mission records.
  • Visual Studio Code: Development environment and code editor.
  • VS Code Live Server: Local website testing.

The project was developed and tested on a personal computer using a web browser and an internet connection for external resources.

How is the project creative?

SpaceVerse presents space exploration through the idea of a digital space museum. Instead of focusing only on successful launches and mission achievements, it explores the stories that continue after the final communication signal. Its combination of a searchable archive, destination-based exploration, historical imagery, immersive visual design and educational quizzes makes the subject more engaging and accessible.

What factors did the team consider?

The project considered historical accuracy, reliability of research sources, accessibility, educational value and responsible presentation of scientific information. Mission status and resting-place descriptions use cautious wording when exact information is unavailable. It also distinguishes between equipment left on planetary surfaces, spacecraft travelling through deep space and defunct objects in Earth orbit, since they do not represent the same environmental concerns.

SpaceVerse ultimately aims to remind visitors that a mission's end does not mean the end of its scientific or historical story.
